overview.intro: In the 6th century BCE, two great religious movements - Jainism and Buddhism - arose in north-eastern India as protests against the complexity and cost of Vedic ritual and the rigidity of the varna order. This chapter studies their sacred literature (the Angas, the Tripitikas and the Jatakas), the social and economic causes that made them flourish, and their central doctrines: the Tri-ratnas, Karma, Equality and Moksha in Jainism; the Four Noble Truths, the Eight-fold Path and Nirvana in Buddhism.

blocks.text: The 6th century BCE was an age of ferment. Iron agriculture had produced surplus and trade; new towns grew along the Ganga; sixteen mahajanapadas competed for power. The old Vedic religion had become ritual-heavy and expensive, and the Brahmans' supremacy resented by the rising Kshatriya rulers and trading Vaishya classes. Into this world Mahavira (Vardhamana, c. 540-468 BCE, of the Jnatrika clan near Vaishali) and Gautama Buddha (Siddhartha, c. 566-486 BCE, of the Shakya clan of Kapilavastu) preached simple, ethical religions in the people's own language (Prakrit/Pali), without costly sacrifices or priestly monopoly. Both accepted Karma and rebirth and the goal of liberation, and both upheld ahimsa.

Sources of Jainism and Buddhism. Jainism's sacred canon is the Angas - twelve books recording the words of Mahavira as compiled by his disciple Gandhara disciples in the Prakrit language; they are the earliest substantial Jain literature. Buddhism's canon is the Tripitaka ('three baskets'): the Vinaya Pitaka (monastic discipline), the Sutta Pitaka (the Buddha's discourses) and the Abhidhamma Pitaka (philosophy), preserved in Pali. The Jatakas - over five hundred stories of the Buddha's former births - are attached to the Sutta Pitaka and are precious evidence of everyday life, trade and society in the age. (Brief mention at this level.)

Causes for their rise in the 6th century BCE. Religious: Vedic sacrifices had become elaborate, costly and led by Brahmans in Sanskrit the people could not follow; the religion needed a simpler, ethical core. Social: the varna system had grown rigid and unjust, humiliating the lower orders and women; Kshatriya rulers resented Brahman supremacy, and the new moneyed classes wanted a religion that matched their status. Economic: agriculture with iron ploughs, cattle wealth, and expanding trade created prosperity that both religions (with their emphasis on non-violence and honest dealing) channelled; animal sacrifices clashed with cattle-based agrarian economy. Linguistic: both teachers preached in Prakrit/Pali - languages of the people - not Sanskrit. Personal: the example and organising genius of Mahavira and the Buddha themselves.

Jainism - Tri-ratnas. Jainism teaches that the soul can be freed only through the 'three jewels': Right Faith (samyak darshana) - belief in the truths taught by the Tirthankaras; Right Knowledge (samyak jnana) - correct understanding of reality, including that the universe is eternal and every living being has a soul; and Right Conduct (samyak charitra) - living by five vows: ahimsa (non-injury), satya (truth), asteya (non-stealing), aparigraha (non-possession) and brahmacharya (self-control). Right conduct is impossible without the first two.

Jainism - Karma, Equality, Moksha. Karma in Jainism is almost material: every deed - especially injury to life - coats the soul with fine matter, binding it to the wheel of rebirth; only by stopping further karma (samvara) and shedding old karma (nijara) can the soul rise. Equality: Jainism rejected the superiority of any varna - all souls, high or low, are equal in their capacity for liberation (though, in practice, women faced debate in its monastic orders). Moksha: when all karma is shed the soul, freed, rises to the summit of the universe (Siddhashila) in eternal knowledge and bliss - liberation, not union with a creator, for Jainism accepts no creator god. Mahavira's own life - renouncing home at 30, twelve years of austerity, enlightenment at 42 - embodied the path.

Buddhism - the Four Noble Truths. The Buddha's first sermon at Sarnath set out the Four Noble Truths: (1) the world is full of suffering (dukkha); (2) the cause of suffering is desire (trishna/tanha) - craving for pleasure and possession; (3) suffering can be ended by ending desire; (4) the way to end desire is the Middle Path - the Eight-fold Path - avoiding both luxury and severe self-torture.

Buddhism - the Eight-fold Path and Nirvana. The Eight-fold Path (Ashtangika Marga) consists of Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration - an ethical programme for layperson and monk alike. Following it extinguishes craving; the result is Nirvana - literally 'blowing out' - the end of desire, hatred and delusion, and thus of rebirth: perfect peace. The Buddha denied both the authority of the Vedas and animal sacrifice, admitted women to the Sangha (at Ananda's plea, through Mahaprajapati Gautami), and preached equality: birth does not make one high or low, action does.

The appeal of the two religions. Both religions spoke the people's language, taught in simple ethical terms, rejected caste privilege in spiritual life, ran organised monastic orders (Sangha) that gave dignity to all who joined, and won royal patronage (Bimbisara and Ajatashatru of Magadha; later Chandragupta Maurya for Jainism, Ashoka for Buddhism). Merchants and artisans, the wealth of the new towns, became their chief lay supporters - which is why both spread first along the trade routes.

items: Mahavira (Vardhamana) - 24th and last Tirthankara; born c. 540 BCE at Kundagrama near Vaishali; enlightened at 42; taught the Tri-ratnas.

Gautama Buddha (Siddhartha) - Born c. 566 BCE at Lumbini in the Shakya republic of Kapilavastu; left home (mahabhinishkramana), enlightened at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath (Dharmachakra-pravartana), died (parinirvana) at Kushinagar.
Mahaprajapati Gautami - The Buddha's foster mother; first woman admitted to the Buddhist Sangha.
Bimbisara and Ajatashatru - Kings of Magadha who patronised both religions in their youth of growth.
Vedic religion had become ritualistic, expensive and Brahman-dominated.
Sanskrit was unintelligible to the common people.
The rigid varna system bred social resentment.
Rising Kshatriya and Vaishya classes sought religions without priestly monopoly.
Animal sacrifices conflicted with agrarian cattle economy and the new ideal of ahimsa.
Preaching in Prakrit/Pali reached the masses directly.
Monastic orders (Sangha) spread education and ethics across India.
Royal patronage (e.g., Ashoka) carried Buddhism beyond India to Asia.
Pali and Prakrit literatures (Tripitaka, Jatakas, Jain Angas) enriched Indian languages.
Ahimsa became a permanent strand of Indian ethics, influencing later reformers.

blocks.text: Jainism vs Buddhism: Jainism believes every living being has an eternal individual soul and stresses extreme ahimsa and austerity; Buddhism denies a permanent soul (anatta), follows the Middle Path, and centres on ending desire to attain Nirvana.
Tri-ratnas vs Eight-fold Path: Jainism's three jewels (faith, knowledge, conduct) versus Buddhism's eight practical steps from view to concentration.
Moksha (Jainism) vs Nirvana (Buddhism): Liberated soul rising to Siddhashila in eternal bliss versus the blowing out of craving and the end of rebirth.
Angas vs Tripitaka: The twelve canonical books of the Jains versus the Buddhist 'three baskets' of Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma.

items: Saying Jainism believes in one creator God - it does not; the universe is eternal and uncreated.
Confusing the Tri-ratnas with the Eight-fold Path.
Writing 'Tripitaka' as 'Tripitikas' or mixing up its three baskets.
Claiming the Buddha accepted the Vedas - he denied their authority.

questions.prompt: Mention any two causes for the rise of Jainism and Buddhism in the 6th century BCE.
questions.answer: Any two of: Vedic sacrifices had become elaborate, costly and Brahman-dominated; Sanskrit was unintelligible to the masses; the varna system had become rigid and unjust; Kshatriya and Vaishya classes resented priestly supremacy; animal sacrifice clashed with agrarian cattle economy; both teachers preached in people's languages (Prakrit/Pali).
questions.commonMistake: Naming only personal factors without social context.

questions.prompt: What is meant by Nirvana in Buddhism?
questions.answer: Literally 'blowing out' - the extinction of desire, hatred and delusion, which ends suffering and the cycle of rebirth, giving perfect peace. It is attained by following the Eight-fold Path.
questions.explanation: Define and link to the Path.

questions.answer: Jainism holds that every living being possesses an eternal individual soul, and stresses extreme ahimsa (even involuntary injury binds karma) and austerity; it accepts no creator god, and liberation (moksha) means the soul rising to Siddhashila in eternal bliss. Buddhism denies a permanent soul (anatta), rejects extreme austerity for the Middle Path, and seeks Nirvana - the extinguishing of craving - through the Eight-fold Path. Jainism's canon is the Angas in Prakrit; Buddhism's is the Tripitaka in Pali with the Jatakas. Both, however, reject Vedic authority and caste privilege in spiritual life and uphold ahimsa.
questions.explanation: Soul, path, goal and canon on both sides.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: Jainism and Buddhism spread rapidly among traders and townspeople.
questions.answer: The new towns' merchant and artisan classes were wealthy but ranked low in ritual hierarchy; both religions offered them spiritual equality and dignity. Their ethics - honesty, non-violence, fair dealing - suited commercial life, and monasteries on trade routes served as rest-houses and credit networks, binding merchants to the Sangha. Royal patronage protected the orders along these very routes. Preaching in Prakrit and Pali, the religions spoke the traders' languages, not Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: Social, economic and linguistic reasons together.

questions.prompt: Explain the causes for the rise of Jainism and Buddhism in the 6th century BCE.
questions.answer: Religious: Vedic religion had degenerated into elaborate, expensive sacrifice (yajna) conducted by Brahmans in Sanskrit the people could not follow; genuine ethical teaching was buried under ritual. Social: the varna system had grown rigid and unjust, humiliating the lower orders and women; the Kshatriya rulers resented Brahman supremacy, and the prospering Vaishya classes wanted a religion matching their economic importance. Economic: iron-plough agriculture and expanding trade created a new urban wealth; animal sacrifice wasted cattle vital to the agrarian economy, and the ideal of ahimsa answered this need. Linguistic: both Mahavira and the Buddha preached in Prakrit/Pali - the tongues of the people - making their message directly accessible. Intellectual: the age's questioning spirit (Upanishadic thought) welcomed new doctrines. Finally, the personal example and organising ability of the two founders turned protest into lasting religions.
questions.explanation: Religious, social, economic, linguistic, intellectual + personal.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only one or two causes without development.

questions.prompt: Arrange in order and identify: (1) Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, (2) Birth at Lumbini, (3) First sermon at Sarnath, (4) Parinirvana at Kushinagar.
questions.answer: Correct order: (2) Birth at Lumbini (c. 566 BCE) -> (1) Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (c. 531 BCE) -> (3) First sermon at Sarnath -> (4) Parinirvana at Kushinagar (c. 486 BCE).
questions.commonMistake: Placing the first sermon before enlightenment.
